papers.source_body_en: Promoting increased consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables remains a cornerstone of global public health strategies aimed at preventing noncommunicable diseases and addressing micronutrient deficiencies. However, the safety of fresh produce continues to be challenged by contamination with human enteric pathogens. The persistence and dissemination of human pathogens within agricultural ecosystems represent a complex interplay between microbial physiology, plant-associated niches, environmental stressors, and crop management practices. Following the insights gathered in Volume I of this Research Topic, Volume II brings together four contributions that advance our understanding of these dynamics. Together, these studies reveal how biological adaptation, produce surface characteristics, and environmental reservoirs influence the persistence, transmission, and control of human pathogens and antimicrobial resistance within agricultural systems.A foundational element of pathogen persistence is the ability of human enteric bacteria to adapt to non-host, plant-associated environments. In their comprehensive review, Han et al. (2025) synthesize the metabolic adaptations utilized by Salmonella enterica to survive and colonize plant tissues and agricultural substrates. The authors delineate how S. enterica dynamically reprograms its central carbon and nitrogen metabolism in response to nutrients available in root exudates, leaf apoplastic fluids, and plant tissues. enterica prioritizes glucose metabolism through glycolysis, shifts to gluconeogenesis under sugar-limiting conditions, and exploits alternative carbon sources such as glycerol, fatty acids, and organic acids. Furthermore, de novo amino acid biosynthesis, particularly cysteine via sulfate assimilation, emerges as an indispensable metabolic hub required for bacterial fitness across diverse plant hosts and stress conditions. By highlighting this metabolic plasticity, Han et al. (2025) provide insights into how human pathogens exploit plant metabolic niches, identifying physiological vulnerabilities that could be targeted to prevent preharvest colonization.Interactions at the plant surface are relevant for pathogen attachment, retention, and susceptibility to post-harvest sanitation. Addressing this physical interface, Lightbown and DiCaprio (2025) investigated the impact of leafy green microscale surface topography on the recovery and chemical sanitizer inactivation of Tulane virus (TV), a surrogate for human norovirus. Comparing fresh romaine lettuce and spinach leaves across growth stages and leaf axes, the authors demonstrated that spinach leaf maturity significantly influences chemical inactivation: younger leaves allowed higher viral inactivation by sodium hypochlorite than older leaves. Crucially, the authors engineered polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) topomimetic artificial leaf surfaces ("replicasts") to decouple physical structural attributes from biological variability. By modulating replicast hydrophobicity with lowconcentration surfactants, the artificial surfaces faithfully reproduced viral recovery trends observed on fresh plant tissue, validating topomimetic replicasts as standardized physical tools for produce safety research.Expanding this physical engineering framework to soft fruits, Lightbown and DiCaprio (2026) evaluated PDMS topomimetic artificial surfaces modeled after blueberries, strawberries, and raspberries. Soft berries present intricate surface features, ranging from smooth epicuticular wax on blueberries to achene pits on strawberries and dense trichomes on raspberry drupelets, that create micro-refuges protecting viruses from post-harvest wash treatments. Their findings demonstrated that berry type markedly dictates viral retention, with raspberries retaining higher viral titers than blueberries or strawberries. Surface replicasts of all three berry types closely mirrored the recovery levels obtained from fresh fruits, confirming that physical micro-architecture is a primary driver of viral adhesion and protection against sanitizer wash solutions. These data indicate that while berry replicasts may have utility in modeling surface adhesion of viruses to berries and in viral recovery studies, they are not suitable for studies of viral inactivation by chemical sanitizers.Beyond pathogen persistence and sanitizer efficacy, agricultural environments are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), introducing an additional dimension to produce safety risk assessment. (2025) conducted whole-genome sequencing on 87 multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial strains isolated from leafy greens, root zone soil, and bulk soil within urban agriculture systems. Representing 14 genera dominated by Pseudomonas, Serratia, Providencia, and Bacillus, these environmental isolates exhibited extensive resistomes primarily encoding multidrug efflux systems, β-lactamases, and tetracycline resistance determinants. All MDR isolates harbored mobile genetic elements (MGEs), with multiple antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) located in close physical proximity (<5 kb) to transposons, plasmids, or prophages. These findings support the notion that urban agricultural soils and fresh produce can act as environmental reservoirs and potential mobilization vectors for AMR elements, emphasizing the necessity of monitoring resistome dynamics alongside conventional foodborne pathogens.Overall, these studies demonstrate that both biological adaptation and environmental context shape the persistence, transmission, and control of food safety hazards in agricultural systems. Importantly, these findings also underscore how crop-management decisions may influence foodsafety risks across production systems. Deciphering bacterial metabolic flexibility, standardizing physical produce surface models for viral wash treatments, and mapping environmental resistomes in urban agroecosystems collectively inform risk assessment, agronomic policy, and post-harvest intervention protocols. (2025) highlight the remarkable metabolic adaptability of S. enterica to plant-associated environments, suggesting that differences in plant genotypes and their associated nutrient profiles may influence pathogen colonization potential. Lightbown andDiCaprio (2025, 2026) demonstrate that harvest maturity, produce type, and post-harvest washing practices affect viral retention and sanitizer efficacy through differences in surface architecture. Likewise, Harrelson et al. (2025) show that urban agricultural soils and produce can serve as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance, emphasizing the importance of understanding how management practices, including irrigation and soil amendment strategies, influence the composition and dissemination of resistance determinants. Together, these management factors interact with environmental conditions, including moisture, temperature, soil properties, and plant developmental stage, to shape persistence and transmission within agricultural ecosystems. This improved understanding of how enteric pathogens interact with fruit and vegetable production systems moves the field beyond solely exclusionary approaches to food safety and supports the development of more targeted interventions that address the biological and ecological mechanisms underlying pathogen survival. Continued research at the intersection of plant biology, microbiology, and agricultural systems remains essential to advance the safe and sustainable production of fresh fruits and vegetables globally.
papers.abstract_zh: 促进增加新鲜水果和蔬菜的消费仍然是旨在预防非传染性疾病和解决微量营养素缺乏的全球公共卫生战略的基石。然而,新鲜农产品的安全性继续受到人类肠道病原体污染的挑战。人类病原体在农业生态系统中的持续存在和传播代表了微生物生理学、植物相关生态位、环境压力源和作物管理实践之间复杂的相互作用。继本研究主题第一卷中收集的见解之后,第二卷汇集了四项贡献,以增进我们对这些动态的理解。这些研究共同揭示了生物适应、农产品表面特征和环境 储存宿主 如何影响农业系统中人类病原体的持久性、传播 以及对人类病原体和抗菌素耐药性的控制。病原体持久性的一个基本要素是人类肠道细菌适应非 宿主、植物相关环境的能力。在他们的综合评论中,Han 等人。(2025) 合成了肠沙门氏菌用于生存和定植植物组织和农业基质的代谢适应性。作者描述了肠沙门氏菌如何动态地重新编程其中心碳和氮代谢,以响应根分泌物、叶质外体液和植物组织中可用的营养物质。Enterica 优先通过糖酵解进行葡萄糖代谢,在糖限制条件下转向糖异生,并利用甘油、脂肪酸和有机酸等替代碳源。此外,从头氨基酸生物合成,特别是通过硫酸盐同化的半胱氨酸,成为细菌适应不同植物 宿主 和胁迫条件所需的不可或缺的代谢中心。通过强调这种代谢可塑性,Han 等人。(2025) 提供了关于人类病原体如何利用植物代谢生态位的见解,确定了可以预防收获前定殖的生理脆弱性。植物表面的相互作用与病原体的附着、保留和对收获后卫生的敏感性相关。针对这一物理界面,Lightbown 和 DiCaprio (2025) 研究了绿叶微型表面形貌对杜兰病毒 (TV)(人类 诺如病毒 的替代品)恢复和化学消毒剂灭活的影响。作者通过比较新鲜的生菜和菠菜叶子的生长阶段和叶轴,发现菠菜叶子的成熟度显着影响化学灭活:较老的叶子相比,较老的叶子更容易被次氯酸钠灭活。至关重要的是,作者设计了聚二甲基硅氧烷(PDMS)拓扑模拟人造叶子表面(“复制品”),以将物理结构属性与生物变异性分开。通过用低浓度表面活性剂调节复制体的疏水性,人造表面忠实地再现了在新鲜植物组织上观察到的病毒恢复趋势,验证了拓扑模拟复制体作为生产安全研究的标准化物理工具。将这种物理工程框架扩展到软水果,Lightbown 和 DiCaprio (2026) 评估了以蓝莓、草莓和覆盆子为模型的 PDMS 拓扑模拟人造表面。柔软的浆果呈现出复杂的表面特征,从蓝莓上光滑的表皮蜡到草莓上的瘦果核,再到覆盆子核果上密集的毛状体,这些特征形成了微避难所,保护病毒免受采后清洗 治疗 的侵害。他们的研究结果表明,浆果类型显着决定了病毒的保留,覆盆子比蓝莓或草莓保留了更高的病毒滴度。所有三种浆果类型的表面复制品都密切反映了从新鲜水果中获得的恢复水平,证实物理微结构是病毒粘附和针对消毒剂清洗溶液的保护的主要驱动因素。这些数据表明,虽然浆果复制体可能有助于模拟病毒对浆果的表面粘附和病毒回收研究,但它们不适合研究化学消毒剂对病毒的灭活。除了病原体持久性和消毒剂功效之外,农业环境越来越被认为是抗菌素耐药性(AMR)的储存宿主,引入了额外的维度来进行安全风险评估。(2025) 对从城市农业系统内的绿叶蔬菜、根区土壤和大块土壤中分离出的 87 种多重耐药 (MDR) 细菌菌株进行了全 基因组 测序。这些环境分离株代表以假单胞菌属、沙雷氏菌属、普罗维登斯氏菌属和芽孢杆菌属为主的 14 个属,表现出广泛的耐药组,主要编码多药外排系统、β-内酰胺酶和四环素耐药决定簇。所有 MDR 分离株都含有可移动遗传元件 (MGE),其中多个抗生素抗性基因 (ARG) 与转座子、质粒或前噬菌体物理位置非常接近 (<5 kb)。这些发现支持这样的观点,即城市农业土壤和新鲜农产品可以充当环境储存宿主和AMR元素的潜在动员媒介,强调了与传统食源性病原体一起监测抗药性动态的必要性。总体而言,这些研究表明,生物适应和环境背景塑造了农业系统中食品安全危害的持久性、媒介和控制。重要的是,这些发现还强调了作物管理决策如何影响整个生产系统的食品安全风险。破译细菌代谢灵活性、标准化病毒清洗 治疗 的物理产品表面模型以及绘制城市农业生态系统中的环境抗性组图,共同为风险评估、农艺政策和收获后干预方案提供信息。(2025) 强调了肠沙门氏菌对植物相关环境的显着代谢适应性,表明植物基因型及其相关营养成分的差异可能会影响病原体定植潜力。Lightbown 和 DiCaprio(2025、2026)证明,收获成熟度、农产品类型和收获后清洗做法通过表面结构的差异影响病毒保留和消毒剂功效。同样,哈里森等人。(2025)表明城市农业土壤和农产品可以作为抗菌素耐药性的储存宿主,强调了解管理实践(包括灌溉和土壤改良策略)如何影响耐药性决定因素的组成和传播的重要性。这些管理因素与环境条件(包括湿度、温度、土壤性质和植物发育阶段)相互作用,从而形成农业生态系统中的持久性和传播。对肠道病原体如何与水果和蔬菜生产系统相互作用的认识的提高,使该领域超越了食品安全的单一排除方法,并支持开发更有针对性的干预措施,以解决病原体生存的生物和生态机制。植物生物学、微生物学和农业系统交叉领域的持续研究对于促进全球新鲜水果和蔬菜的安全和可持续生产仍然至关重要。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 该综述重点关注人类 诺如病毒 及其在人类疾病中的作用,特别研究环境和作物管理因素如何影响农业生态系统中这些病原体的持久性、传播 和控制。核心问题是这些因素如何影响人类 诺如病毒 的行为及其引起胃肠炎的可能性。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述汇集了四篇文章,分析了人类病原体与农业系统之间的相互作用。证据包括对肠道沙门氏菌代谢适应、绿叶蔬菜和浆果表面形貌以及城市农业环境中抗菌素耐药性 (AMR) 存在的研究。该综述没有明确报告荟萃分析或汇总估计,而是综合了这些研究的结果。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 该综述的结论是,包括诺如病毒在内的人类病原体的持久性和传播受到生物适应和环境因素的影响。它强调了了解农产品表面特性和环境 储存宿主 如何影响病原体生存的重要性以及对食品安全进行有针对性的干预措施的必要性。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该审查确定了在理解特定作物管理实践如何影响 诺如病毒 持久性和 传播 方面的差距。它还指出,虽然这些研究提供了对环境因素作用的见解,但有关 诺如病毒 基因组或变异对这些动态的直接影响的数据有限。此外,该评论承认需要进一步研究物理表面结构在病毒灭活中的作用。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议,未来的研究应侧重于破译人类病原体的代谢灵活性、标准化病毒清洗 治疗 的农产品表面物理模型,以及绘制城市农业生态系统中的环境抗性组图。这些努力可以为更有效的风险评估策略、农艺政策和收获后干预方案提供信息。

papers.full_text: AbstractFecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an effective therapy for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI) and is increasingly explored for other dysbiosis-related disorders. However, its implementation as a regulated therapeutic strategy requires robust donor screening, biosafety frameworks, and standardized processing workflows. Here, we describe the establishment of the first fecal microbiota biobank in southern Brazil and evaluate the incorporation of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary layer of donor characterization and safety assessment. A structured donor selection pipeline based on international guidelines was implemented, integrating clinical screening, biochemical and serological testing, and microbiological analyses. Of 100 screened candidates, only four donors met all eligibility criteria and were included in the biobank, highlighting the stringency of the selection process. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed a diverse resistome across all donors, including a shared core set of resistance genes alongside marked interindividual variability. Dominant resistance determinants included tetracycline-associated genes, ermF, CfxA-type β-lactamases, and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, which were associated with specific gut taxa. Genomic context analysis further identified four ARG-containing contigs with features compatible with potential mobility, although active horizontal gene transfer was beyond the scope of this study. Notably, tet(Q) and ermF were predominantly associated with Bacteroides fragilis, supporting its role as a reservoir of resistance determinants in the gut microbiota. These findings support the use of metagenomic profiling as a complementary approach to donor characterization and risk assessment rather than as a standalone criterion for donor exclusion. Overall, this study provides a framework for microbiota biobank implementation and highlights the potential of metagenomic analysis to complement conventional biosafety screening in FMT.Keywords: antimicrobial resistance, biosafety, fecal microbiota transplantation, metagenomics, microbiota-based therapies, resistome 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study designThis study was designed as a descriptive and methodological investigation aimed at establishing the first fecal microbiota biobank in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, intended to support the future clinical use of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in selected diseases. The study was structured in three main sequential phases: (i) development of donor screening tools based on international guidelines; (ii) implementation of a clinical and laboratory-based donor selection pipeline; and (iii) exploratory incorporation of metagenomic analysis of donor’s fecal microbiota.2.2.Development of donor screening questionnaire and testing pipelineInitially, a comprehensive literature review was performed to identify and compare current recommendations for FMT donor selection and biosafety. This review focused on three core components: clinical exclusion criteria, blood and serological testing, and microbiological screening of fecal samples. The screening tests developed by major national and international working groups were analyzed and compared, including those from the IAG HC-UFMG (Terra et al., 2020), the Netherlands Working Group (Terveer et al., 2020), the International Consensus Conference on FMT (Cammarota et al., 2019), the European FMT Working Group (Cammarota et al., 2017), and the Australian Consensus (Haifer et al., 2020). Based on this comparative analysis and additional literature, a customized screening questionnaire and testing pipeline were developed and implemented in the present work (Supplementary Tables 1, 2).2.3.Donor recruitment and clinical screeningDonor recruitment was conducted between July and September 2023 through public calls and institutional communication channels. Eligible volunteers were invited to complete a structured clinical screening questionnaire based on international FMT guidelines. Eligible donors were required to be between 18 and 50 years of age. Candidates presenting one or more exclusion criteria were not allowed to proceed to subsequent screening steps. Exclusion criteria included, but were not limited to, recent antibiotic use, chronic gastrointestinal diseases, metabolic or autoimmune disorders, recent infectious diseases, high-risk behaviors, and abnormal bowel habits. In addition, the clinical screening questionnaire included questions regarding illicit drug use, chronic medication use, occupational exposure to hazardous substances, and other potential risk factors associated with biological, toxicological or chemical exposure.2.4.Laboratory testsCandidates who met the clinical eligibility criteria were submitted to a comprehensive laboratory screening protocol, designed to assess general health status and exclude infectious agents potentially transmissible through fecal microbiota transplantation. Blood-based analyses included a complete blood count, serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium), renal and hepatic function markers (urea, creatinine, AST, ALT, GGT, bilirubin), metabolic and nutritional parameters (glucose, vitamin B12, folic acid, vitamin D), and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein). Serological screening comprised tests for HIV types I and II, hepatitis A (IgM/IgG), hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG/IgM), hepatitis C (anti-HCV), human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV I/II), cytomegalovirus (IgG/IgM), and Epstein–Barr virus (IgG/IgM).Fecal samples were analyzed for enteric pathogens using conventional microbiological methods and molecular assays. These included coproculture and PCR-based detection of Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) toxin A/B, rotavirus, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, herpes simplex virus I and II (IgG and IgM), and a multiplex PCR panel (FilmArray®) targeting bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens, such as Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., Shigella/EIEC, Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica, C. difficile, Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora cayetanensis, norovirus GI/GII, astrovirus, sapovirus, and adenovirus F40/41. Only candidates presenting normal results across all clinical, serological, biochemical, and microbiological tests were considered eligible donors for inclusion in the biobank.2.5.Processing and storage of fecal materialFecal material from eligible donors was processed under controlled laboratory conditions following standardized operating procedures. Prior to collection, eligible donors received a standardized collection kit containing sterile collection containers, disposable gloves, identification labels, and detailed written instructions describing the collection procedure and emphasizing aseptic handling practices. Donors were instructed to avoid contact between fecal material and external surfaces by using a single-use stool collection device (ColOff®) and to maintain samples refrigerated until transport to the laboratory. Samples were collected from donors’ homes shortly after evacuation and transported to the laboratory in insulated coolers containing ice packs. The total time elapsed between stool passage and laboratory processing did not exceed 6 hours. Upon arrival, samples were processed under atmospheric conditions in a laminar flow cabinet. Fecal material was homogenized in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), filtered through a sterile sieve to remove particulate debris, aliquoted into 10 mL fractions, and stored at −80 °C until use. All samples were labeled and documented to ensure traceability, and storage conditions were continuously monitored.2.6.Shotgun metagenomics sequencingTotal genomic DNA from fecal samples obtained from eligible donors was extracted using the Quick-DNATM HMW MagBead Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), while DNA purity was assessed by NanoVue spectrophotometry (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) based on the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios. DNA integrity was evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis prior to library preparation.Metagenomic sequencing libraries were prepared using the Rapid Barcoding Kit 24 v14 (SQK-RBK114.24; Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK), pooled, and sequenced for 48 h on a MinION device using an R10.4.1 flow cell. Raw reads were basecalled and demultiplexed using Guppy v4.3.0 (Oxford Nanopore Technologies). No extraction blank or negative sequencing control was included in the sequencing workflow.2.7.Identification of antimicrobial resistance genesAntimicrobial resistance determinants were identified directly from sequencing reads using the command-line version of the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI, v6.0.3) against the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD). Read quality was evaluated using NanoPlot v1.40.0, followed by quality filtering using NanoFilt v2.8.0, retaining reads with a minimum mean quality score of Q10 and a minimum length of 500 bp. Only Perfect and Strict hits were retained for downstream analyses, whereas Loose hits were excluded to reduce the likelihood of false-positive assignments. Gene presence/absence, relative abundance, and cumulative abundance profiles were generated for descriptive comparisons across samples using R v4.3.2. Due to the exploratory nature of the study and the limited number of samples, no inferential statistical analyses were performed.2.8.Genomic context and potential mobility of resistance determinantsTo characterize the genomic context of ARGs and assess their potential mobility, sequencing reads were filtered at minimum mean quality score of Q8 and a minimum length of 1000 bp and were assembled using Flye v2.9.6. The resulting contigs were screened for ARGs using ABRicate v1.4.0 against the CARD database (≥90% identity and ≥80% coverage), and ARG-containing contigs were further characterized for plasmid association and mobility-related features using geNomad v1.12.0, MOB-suite v3.1.9, Bakta v1.9.4, and ISEScan v1.7.3. To assess sequence support for candidate contigs and ARGs, the reads were mapped to the corresponding Flye assemblies using Minimap2 v2.31, and read depth was calculated with SAMtools v1.23.1.2.9.Data availabilityThe raw sequencing data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1499213.2.10.Ethical considerationsThe study was approved by the institutional review board under process number CAAE: 42603020.0.0000.0121. All participants provided written informed consent prior to sample collection and laboratory analyses. 2.1.Study designThis study was designed as a descriptive and methodological investigation aimed at establishing the first fecal microbiota biobank in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, intended to support the future clinical use of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in selected diseases. The study was structured in three main sequential phases: (i) development of donor screening tools based on international guidelines; (ii) implementation of a clinical and laboratory-based donor selection pipeline; and (iii) exploratory incorporation of metagenomic analysis of donor’s fecal microbiota. 2.5.Processing and storage of fecal materialFecal material from eligible donors was processed under controlled laboratory conditions following standardized operating procedures. Prior to collection, eligible donors received a standardized collection kit containing sterile collection containers, disposable gloves, identification labels, and detailed written instructions describing the collection procedure and emphasizing aseptic handling practices. Donors were instructed to avoid contact between fecal material and external surfaces by using a single-use stool collection device (ColOff®) and to maintain samples refrigerated until transport to the laboratory. Samples were collected from donors’ homes shortly after evacuation and transported to the laboratory in insulated coolers containing ice packs. The total time elapsed between stool passage and laboratory processing did not exceed 6 hours. Upon arrival, samples were processed under atmospheric conditions in a laminar flow cabinet. Fecal material was homogenized in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), filtered through a sterile sieve to remove particulate debris, aliquoted into 10 mL fractions, and stored at −80 °C until use. All samples were labeled and documented to ensure traceability, and storage conditions were continuously monitored. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frabi.2026.1905540/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 3.Results3.1.Donor recruitment and clinical eligibilityA total of 100 candidates were included in the clinical screening questionnaire during the recruitment period. Of these, 6 candidates met the clinical eligibility criteria and were referred to laboratory screening. Following biochemical, serological, and microbiological screening, two additional candidates were excluded, one due to the detection of toxigenic C. difficile by multiplex PCR (FilmArray®), while another candidate did not complete the laboratory screening process. Therefore, four participants were ultimately considered eligible for fecal microbiota donation and inclusion in the biobank. The donor selection workflow and the main exclusion criteria identified are illustrated in Figure 1. The demographic characteristics of the eligible donors are summarized in Supplementary Table 3.Figure 1Flowchart illustrating the multistep donor selection process.Flowchart detailing donor screening for a biobank. From one hundred questionnaires, six proceed to clinical evaluation and laboratory testing. Two are excluded due to C. difficile detection and incomplete screening, leading to four eligible donors. Main exclusion criteria are also listed.3.2.Resistome profile characterizationSequencing generated 7.09 Gb of data across all samples (5.44 million reads; N50 = 2.55 kb), with read accuracy ranging from 79.6% to 84.7%, indicating overall good sequencing performance. These genes were strongly associated with specific bacterial taxa, indicating clear links between resistome composition and microbiota structure. In particular, tet(Q) was predominantly associated with Bacteroides fragilis, while tet(W) was mainly linked to Bifidobacterium longum. The gene tet(O) was primarily associated with Campylobacter jejuni, whereas ErmF was also largely attributed to Bacteroides fragilis. In contrast, CfxA2 was associated with Prevotella intermedia, highlighting additional taxonomic contributors to β-lactam resistance.Figure 3(A) Individual bar plots for each sample showing the distribution (%) of the 12 most abundant resistance genes, categorized by their associated bacterial taxa. The color legend indicates taxonomic group carrying the detected ARGs. (B) Stacked bar plot illustrating the distribution of 12 most abundant ARGs across all samples. Each color represents a specific ARG.Panel A shows four grouped bar charts, one for each sample, displaying relative abundance percentages of taxa co-occurring with different antibiotic resistance genes, color-coded by species. Panel B shows a stacked bar graph comparing the relative abundance percentages of different antibiotic resistance genes across the same four samples, with each gene represented by a distinct color.Although these genes were detected across all samples, their proportional abundance varied markedly (Figure 3B). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionA central challenge in FMT implementation worldwide remains the identification of suitable donors. Our findings confirm that donor selection is a highly restrictive process, with only a minority of screened candidates ultimately qualifying for donation. Similar donor approval rates have been reported in international biobanking initiatives, reflecting the stringency required to minimize transmissible risks (Cammarota et al., 2017; Terra et al., 2020). This reinforces the importance of structured, transparent, and reproducible selection workflows as a foundational element of any FMT program. By integrating clinical questionnaires, biochemical and serological testing, and microbiological screening, our workflow aligns with major international guidelines while being operationally feasible within public and private healthcare infrastructures in Brazil (Cammarota et al., 2019). This aspect is particularly relevant in low- and middle-income countries, where the implementation of microbiota-based therapies often faces infrastructural and regulatory barriers.An important contribution of this study is the incorporation of metagenomic sequencing and ARG profiling as an additional source of information for potential donor–recipient selection and risk assessment. In this work, we identified antimicrobial resistance determinants involving clinically relevant antibiotic classes, such as tetracyclines and aminoglycosides, within major members of the gut microbiota, with some occurring in genomic contexts compatible with potential mobilization, even among donors who had undergone rigorous screening.As expected, tetracycline resistance determinants such as tet(Q) and tet(W) were highly prevalent and primarily associated with Bacteroides fragilis and Bifidobacterium longum, respectively, reinforcing the well-established role of these taxa as major reservoirs of tetracycline resistance in the human gut (Shoemaker et al., 2001; Hu et al., 2013). The relatively high abundance of ermF, a gene associated with cross-resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramin B antibiotics (MLSb phenotype), and linked to Bacteroides fragilis, further highlights the role of this species as a reservoir of resistance determinants (Shoemaker et al., 2001). Notably, tet(Q) and ermF occurred together in a chromosomal context containing an IS30 family transposase in Sample 3, sharing features with resistance architectures described in Bacteroides conjugative transposons, including the CTnDOT family, which carries both determinants and contains regions involved in mobilization and conjugative transfer (Shoemaker et al., 2001; Jeters et al., 2009). Other tet(Q) and ARG containing contigs showed complementary features compatible with potential mobility, including proximity to conjugative transfer machinery and association with circular plasmid contigs containing plasmid replication, recombination, or relaxase features. Together, these findings indicate that some resistance determinants occurred in genomic environments compatible with potential mobilization; however, assessment of active horizontal gene transfer was beyond the scope of this study.Although the mobility and horizontal transfer of ARGs are important concerns, the potential for bacteria carrying ARGs in donor feces to persist, translocate, and cause infection in immunocompromised recipients should not be overlooked. This concern is illustrated by the seminal work of DeFilipp et al., which traced the transmission of an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli from donor material to a recipient who subsequently developed bacteremia and died (DeFilipp et al., 2019). In contrast, Woodworth et al. showed that FMT can also promote sustained decolonization of multidrug-resistant organisms, with replacement of baseline ESBL-producing bacteria by susceptible strains (Woodworth et al., 2023). These contrasting findings suggest that the clinical implications of ARGs in FMT depend on the broader donor–recipient context, including the bacterial host and genomic context, but particularly the recipient’s clinical condition and anticipated antimicrobial exposure.In this context, ARG profiling could be used as a complementary layer of donor–recipient assessment rather than as an exclusion criterion, helping to identify cases that may warrant further investigation through phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing or deeper genomic characterization. For example, when clinically relevant resistance determinants are identified, decision makers could consider further investigation of donor feces based on existing guidance for surveillance of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria in health care settings (World Health Organization, 2017) This approach could potentially be extended to ESBL producing organisms until further studies specifically evaluating antimicrobial resistance related risks in FMT become available. Future longitudinal studies integrating donor–recipient metagenomic profiling, strain tracking, and clinical outcomes will be important to determine how donor resistance profiles influence the clinical effects of FMT and to refine this risk assessment approach.Beyond donor screening, alternative FMT formulations may provide complementary strategies to improve biosafety. Sterile fecal filtrates and defined microbial consortia, for example, do not rely on the transfer of viable bacterial communities and may therefore reduce some of the risks associated with the introduction of donor-derived organisms (Ott et al., 2017; Feuerstadt et al., 2022). Early clinical evidence suggests that some of these approaches may retain therapeutic efficacy, although their safety and effectiveness require validation in larger and more diverse clinical settings (Ott et al., 2017; Kao et al., 2025). Together, approaches that combine improved biosafety with greater standardization may facilitate the broader and safer implementation of microbiota-based therapies.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionFecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has consolidated itself as one of the most effective therapeutic interventions for rCDI, with success rates exceeding 90% (van Nood et al., 2013; Quraishi et al., 2017). Beyond this indication, FMT has progressively gained attention as a potential therapeutic strategy for a wide spectrum of disorders linked to intestinal dysbiosis, including inflammatory, metabolic, and immune-mediated diseases (Smits et al., 2013; Qu et al., 2022; Soveral et al., 2022).Despite its clinical relevance, FMT poses singular challenges from a technical and safety perspective. Unlike conventional pharmaceuticals or biologics composed of defined molecular entities, FMT involves the transfer of a complex and dynamic biological ecosystem, whose composition and functional attributes remain only partially characterized (Khoruts and Sadowsky, 2016; Vaughn et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2020). This intrinsic complexity complicates standardization, traceability and quality control, fundamental requirements for the development of safe and scalable therapeutic products (Cammarota et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021).In this context, fecal microbiota biorepositories and stool banks have emerged as essential infrastructures for the consolidation of FMT as a regulated therapy. These platforms aim to centralize donor recruitment, ensure standardized screening, enable controlled processing and storage, and support the traceability of material used for clinical application (Terveer et al., 2017; Kragsnaes et al., 2020). However, the implementation of such systems remains heterogeneous across countries, reflecting differences in regulatory environments, technological capacity, and clinical practice (Cammarota et al., 2017; Haifer et al., 2020; Terra et al., 2020).Current donor screening protocols are primarily designed to exclude known pathogens and high-risk clinical conditions (Woodworth et al., 2017). While indispensable, these strategies are limited to predefined targets and do not fully encompass the functional and genetic complexity of donor microbiota (Bibbò et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2026). As FMT expands toward new clinical indications and increasingly vulnerable patient populations, the need for more comprehensive a approaches to biosafety becomes increasingly evident (Ianiro et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2025).Within this, the present study describes the establishment of the first fecal microbiota biobank in Santa Catarina and explores the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary tool for safety assessment, not as a definitive safety criterion, but as a way for expanding quality control strategies in microbiota-based therapies. 2.2.Development of donor screening questionnaire and testing pipelineInitially, a comprehensive literature review was performed to identify and compare current recommendations for FMT donor selection and biosafety. This review focused on three core components: clinical exclusion criteria, blood and serological testing, and microbiological screening of fecal samples. The screening tests developed by major national and international working groups were analyzed and compared, including those from the IAG HC-UFMG (Terra et al., 2020), the Netherlands Working Group (Terveer et al., 2020), the International Consensus Conference on FMT (Cammarota et al., 2019), the European FMT Working Group (Cammarota et al., 2017), and the Australian Consensus (Haifer et al., 2020). Based on this comparative analysis and additional literature, a customized screening questionnaire and testing pipeline were developed and implemented in the present work (Supplementary Tables 1, 2). 2.3.Donor recruitment and clinical screeningDonor recruitment was conducted between July and September 2023 through public calls and institutional communication channels. Eligible volunteers were invited to complete a structured clinical screening questionnaire based on international FMT guidelines. Eligible donors were required to be between 18 and 50 years of age. Candidates presenting one or more exclusion criteria were not allowed to proceed to subsequent screening steps. Exclusion criteria included, but were not limited to, recent antibiotic use, chronic gastrointestinal diseases, metabolic or autoimmune disorders, recent infectious diseases, high-risk behaviors, and abnormal bowel habits. In addition, the clinical screening questionnaire included questions regarding illicit drug use, chronic medication use, occupational exposure to hazardous substances, and other potential risk factors associated with biological, toxicological or chemical exposure. 2.4.Laboratory testsCandidates who met the clinical eligibility criteria were submitted to a comprehensive laboratory screening protocol, designed to assess general health status and exclude infectious agents potentially transmissible through fecal microbiota transplantation. Blood-based analyses included a complete blood count, serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium), renal and hepatic function markers (urea, creatinine, AST, ALT, GGT, bilirubin), metabolic and nutritional parameters (glucose, vitamin B12, folic acid, vitamin D), and inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein). Serological screening comprised tests for HIV types I and II, hepatitis A (IgM/IgG), hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG/IgM), hepatitis C (anti-HCV), human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV I/II), cytomegalovirus (IgG/IgM), and Epstein–Barr virus (IgG/IgM).Fecal samples were analyzed for enteric pathogens using conventional microbiological methods and molecular assays. These included coproculture and PCR-based detection of Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) toxin A/B, rotavirus, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2, herpes simplex virus I and II (IgG and IgM), and a multiplex PCR panel (FilmArray®) targeting bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens, such as Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., Shigella/EIEC, Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica, C. difficile, Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora cayetanensis, norovirus GI/GII, astrovirus, sapovirus, and adenovirus F40/41. Only candidates presenting normal results across all clinical, serological, biochemical, and microbiological tests were considered eligible donors for inclusion in the biobank. 2.6.Shotgun metagenomics sequencingTotal genomic DNA from fecal samples obtained from eligible donors was extracted using the Quick-DNATM HMW MagBead Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), while DNA purity was assessed by NanoVue spectrophotometry (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) based on the A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios. DNA integrity was evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis prior to library preparation.Metagenomic sequencing libraries were prepared using the Rapid Barcoding Kit 24 v14 (SQK-RBK114.24; Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK), pooled, and sequenced for 48 h on a MinION device using an R10.4.1 flow cell. Raw reads were basecalled and demultiplexed using Guppy v4.3.0 (Oxford Nanopore Technologies). No extraction blank or negative sequencing control was included in the sequencing workflow. 2.7.Identification of antimicrobial resistance genesAntimicrobial resistance determinants were identified directly from sequencing reads using the command-line version of the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI, v6.0.3) against the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD). Read quality was evaluated using NanoPlot v1.40.0, followed by quality filtering using NanoFilt v2.8.0, retaining reads with a minimum mean quality score of Q10 and a minimum length of 500 bp. Only Perfect and Strict hits were retained for downstream analyses, whereas Loose hits were excluded to reduce the likelihood of false-positive assignments. papers.full_text: This study provides the first comprehensive description of the clinical phenotype and outcomes of all known patients with the heterozygous IRF4 p.T95R variant. Stojcic et al. analyze 10 affected individuals, identifying shared clinical features, treatment responses, and outcomes, and consider implications for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. IRF4 is a transcription factor within the interferon regulatory factor family that controls key aspects of lymphocyte differentiation and adaptive immunity. The heterozygous IRF4 p.Thr95Arg (p.T95R) variant affecting the DNA-binding domain was recently identified to cause a new inborn error of immunity, but the longitudinal clinical course and therapeutic implications remain incompletely defined. We performed detailed clinical characterization and follow-up of all 10 known patients. Each presented with early-onset combined immunodeficiency characterized by hypo- or agammaglobulinemia and marked susceptibility to opportunistic infections. Pulmonary disease was universal, and gastrointestinal involvement was associated with a more severe clinical course. Four patients underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; two survived, and two died. Notably, both deaths occurred in patients transplanted in the setting of active infection. These findings define IRF4 p.T95R as a profound combined immunodeficiency with high infectious burden and demonstrate that disease severity and intervention timing may contribute to transplant outcomes, supporting early diagnosis and timely transplantation before uncontrolled infection. The top section describes the clinical features associated with IRF4 T95R. It includes icons and text labels indicating conditions such as hypo- or agamma globulinemia, combined immunodeficiency, age of onset less than 1 year, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, gastrointestinal manifestations, herpesviridae infections, and onychomycosis. The middle section shows the distribution of patients who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and those who did not. The bottom section outlines the outcomes of HSCT, including graft loss, death, good outcome, and active infection at HSCT. Each patient's timeline is divided into sections with specific medical conditions, treatments, and outcomes. Family 1, Patient 1. Family 2, Patient 2. Family 3, Patient 3. Family 4, Patient 4. Each family shows a chronological sequence of medical events, treatments, and outcomes for each patient. The timelines include details such as the use of antibiotics, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and other medications, as well as the timing of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Key events are marked with specific dates and descriptions, including the use of treatments like prednisone, rituximab, and tacrolimus. The timelines also highlight the occurrence of infections, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), and other complications. The use of different colors and markers helps to distinguish between respiratory, gastrointestinal, treatment, and transplant-associated events.Transplant approaches were heterogeneous, reflecting disease severity and donor availability, as well as varied local protocols. For their initial HSCT, two patients received matched unrelated donor grafts, and two underwent haploidentical related donor transplantation. One haploidentical recipient received an ex vivo TCRα/β- and CD19-depleted graft, while the other received posttransplant cyclophosphamide–based GVHD prophylaxis. Upfront conditioning regimens were primarily reduced-toxicity conditioning (RTC, 3/4), with myeloablative conditioning (MAC) in P4 (Table 2). 2/4 patients treated with RTC received treosulfan/fludarabine-based conditioning (Treo/Flu), whereas the remaining patient received a combination of treosulfan and busulfan. Salvage regimens were used in P2 following graft failure, including both RTC with Treo/Flu and reduced intensity conditioning with fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and total body irradiation.Engraftment kinetics were generally prompt in successful procedures, with a median time to neutrophil recovery of 13 days (range 10–25 days) and platelet recovery a median of 14 days (range 11–20 days) for the first HSCT. Although donor chimerism exceeding 95% was achieved in all transplanted patients, durable engraftment was not consistently maintained. Primary graft failure or graft loss occurred in two of four patients. P2 required multiple subsequent transplants due to recurrent graft failure, including secondary graft loss in the setting of refractory CMV infection. Bone marrow aspirate following his second HSCT was edematous and necrotic without evidence of significant hematopoietic regeneration, demonstrating that damage to the hematopoietic niche may have contributed to his repeat graft failure. P4 experienced graft loss after the first HSCT and was awaiting re-transplantation at the time of writing. These findings highlight intrinsic challenges in achieving durable engraftment in this disorder.GVHD occurred in all transplanted patients despite prophylaxis. Acute GVHD was universal and frequently involved the skin and GI tract, with additional liver involvement. Severe manifestations included stage 4 lower GI GVHD and multi-organ involvement. One patient developed chronic GVHD with cutaneous depigmentation consistent with vitiligo (23). GVHD-directed therapies were intensive and multimodal (Table 2).Infectious complications were frequent and clinically consequential. Both patients who ultimately died had active infections at the time of HSCT: CMV in one (P2) and Cryptosporidium and norovirus in the other (P3). CMV reactivation and drug-resistant CMV disease contributed to graft failure and required CMV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte therapy in P2. Additional complications in those undergoing HSCT included BK virus–associated hemorrhagic cystitis, bacteremia, fungemia, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy, and multidrug-resistant septicemia.All deaths in this cohort occurred following HSCT and were attributed to active infections at the time of transplant. Collectively, HSCT in four IRF4T95R patients was associated with high rates of graft instability, universal acute GVHD, and substantial infection-related morbidity and mortality. While immune reconstitution was achievable in selected patients, transplant-related toxicity remained a major determinant of outcome. Materials and methodsAll study participants and/or their parents/guardians provided written informed consent for sequencing, data analysis, and publication of findings. Research study protocols were approved by local institutions, specifically the University of British Columbia Clinical Research Ethics Board (H15-00641 and H18-02853); Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile de France II, Paris, France (reference: 2015-01-05; 2015-01-05 MS2); the French Advisory Committee on Data Processing in Medical Research (Comité Consultatif sur le Traitement de l’information en matière de Recherche dans le domaine de la Santé, Paris, France; reference: 15.297bis); the Vanderbilt University Medical Center Human Research Protection Program (Institutional Review Board no.: 200412); the University of Ulm ethics board, Germany (application number 156/11); and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health.All patients were identified by clinical teams to carry the IRF4 p.Thr95Arg variant through next-generation sequencing (NM_002460.4(IRF4):c.284C>G (p.Thr95Arg), ClinVar variation ID: 2987365; accession: VCV002987365.3). Biochemical workup of P1 to P7 was completed previously (22). Comprehensive clinical reports were analyzed to track clinical characteristics associated with each case. Clinical diagnoses were performed according to local guidelines. Classification of conditioning regimens was performed according to the EMBT handbook (41). (22, 23). The published findings of this case are briefly summarized here.P1 was born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents and tolerated all pediatric vaccines, including BCG. Symptom onset was pneumonia at 6 mo, followed by repeated upper respiratory tract infections from 6 mo to 3 years. From age 3–8 years, he continued to have severe recurrent pneumonias, as well as bronchiectasis. At 7 years old, hypogammaglobulinemia with reduced B cells was diagnosed. IgG replacement therapy and prophylactic antimicrobials successfully reduced the frequency of respiratory infections. GI manifestations began at age 3 years with chronic diarrhea and led to worsening abdominal pain from age 11 years onward that partially resolved with prednisone. At age 10 years, P1 developed a non-itchy maculopapular rash on his face, limbs, hands, and feet and tested positive for EBV in peripheral blood.The decision was made to move to HSCT due to the recurrent infections despite conventional therapies. P1 was grafted from a matched unrelated donor at age 13 years. Platelet and neutrophil recovery were achieved at 11 and 12 days after HSCT, respectively. 25 days after HSCT, steroid-refractory grade II acute cutaneous GVHD was diagnosed, which resolved with ruxolitinib. Late-onset hemorrhagic cystitis was attributed to polyomavirus BK. At 80 days after HSCT, P1 presented with thrombocytopenia, successfully treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and thrombopoietin. At 6 mo after HSCT, he presented with chronic cutaneous GVHD and began steroid therapy, with GVHD resolving within 2 mo, but vitiligo depigmentation gradually developing on the face, limbs, and trunk. IVIG replacement therapy was discontinued at 9 mo after HSCT following B cell recovery, and complete donor chimerism was sustained over the 1-year follow-up period. T, B, and NK cells normalized to age-appropriate reference ranges by 30 mo after HSCT. A protective antibody response to hepatitis B vaccination was achieved after HSCT. All immunosuppressants were discontinued by 32 mo after HSCT, except baricitinib, which replaced ruxolitinib at 28 mo after HSCT. As of the last report at 36 mo after HSCT, P1 continued on baricitinib and has remained free of infections and GVHD (23).Family 2, P2P2 was born to nonconsanguineous parents, healthy apart from a maternal history of rheumatoid arthritis. He tolerated all routine immunizations and was otherwise healthy until 11 mo of age, when he presented with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Rhinovirus/enterovirus infection, PJP, CMV viremia, and Escherichia coli ventilator-associated pneumonia ensued. Immunological assessment revealed agammaglobulinemia, low class-switched memory B cells, an undetectable response to vaccination, and reduced lymphocyte proliferation. After treatment of his infections, P2 was started on a regimen of IVIG, cotrimoxazole and valganciclovir prophylaxis. P2 then moved to HSCT due to the overall clinical picture of CID with multidrug-resistant CMV viremia. At 22 mo, he received his first HSCT from a matched unrelated donor, with GVHD prophylaxis of tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). He received his second graft at 31 mo, followed by a replicate infusion at 32 mo. Due to the inability to procure more transplants from the original donor, both were sourced from the haploidentical father with TCR α-β and CD19 depletion. HSCT was repeatedly complicated by graft loss due to ongoing multidrug-resistant CMV and CMV–end organ disease.Since our last report, P2 received his third HSCT at age 33 mo. Respiratory decompensation, SOS, and cutaneous and hepatic GVHD developed. He was treated with positive pressure ventilation, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery for an abscess of the right lower lung, and a chest tube. Microbiology was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus, and pathology showed chronic pneumonitis and bronchopneumonia of multifactorial etiology. Chest tube removal 1 mo later was complicated by pneumothorax. Further assessment revealed colonic grade 1 GVHD, possible lung GVHD, and bronchoscopy positive for CMV and rhinovirus/enterovirus. full_text_sections.results: ResultsIRF4T95R cohort overviewTo date, 10 individuals with the IRF4T95R variant (NM_002460.4(IRF4):c.284C>G (p.Thr95Arg), ClinVar variation ID: 2987365, accession: VCV002987365.3) have been identified. Seven were included in the original report (22), and patients are therefore numbered according to that initial publication. A follow-up clinical report for patient 1 (P1) was recently published by Wang and colleagues, and these results have been incorporated into the present analysis (23). Patients 8, 9, and 10 (P8, P9, and P10) are newly reported in this cohort, having been identified to carry the IRF4T95R variant by next-generation sequencing. P10 is also discussed by Vignesh et al. (unpublished data).Seven of 10 cases are formally documented to have arisen de novo. In one family (F6), the two affected siblings inherited the IRF4T95R variant from their unaffected mosaic mother, and in one family (F9), the father’s genotype is unknown (Table 1 and Fig. 2 A). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis study expands current understanding of the disease course associated with the heterozygous IRF4T95R variant by defining the clinical manifestations and treatment outcomes in 10 affected patients, representing all diagnosed cases (22, 23). As such, this series provides the most comprehensive description currently available of this rare disorder.IRF4 T95R combined immunodeficiency is defined by marked susceptibility to a broad spectrum of infections. Patients are at particularly high risk of morbidity and mortality from opportunistic and viral pathogens, including P. jirovecii, EBV, CMV, and Cryptosporidium. Laboratory investigation demonstrated evidence of combined humoral and cellular immune dysfunction (22, 24) (Table S2). B cell immunity was profoundly impaired, with very low or absent serum antibody levels, reduced total CD19+ B cell numbers, and a marked differentiation arrest characterized by accumulation of naïve B cells and depletion of class-switched memory B cells and plasmablasts. T cell immunity was quantitatively preserved but qualitatively abnormal, with altered subset distribution, reduced Th17 and TFH populations, and impaired cytokine production, including reduced IL-2 and IFN-γ. Together, infection history and laboratory evidence of combined humoral and cellular immune dysfunction support IRF4T95R causing a profound combined immunodeficiency (CID).Clinically, patients exhibited early-onset, severe, and recurrent infections involving multiple organ systems. Respiratory disease was universal, with most patients developing pneumonia within the first year of life, frequently due to P. jirovecii. Additional respiratory complications included bronchiectasis and airway hyperreactivity, underscoring progressive pulmonary involvement as a defining feature. GI manifestations, a recognized component of many IEIs (25, 26), were observed in eight patients, commonly infection-associated. Notably, GI involvement was associated with an overall more severe clinical course, including progression to HSCT, whereas patients without GI disease had comparatively favorable outcomes. This interpretation is, however, limited by the small sample size and circular nature of causality, with it remaining undetermined if underlying GI dysfunction predisposed to infection, or if infection preceded GI dysfunction. It thus remains to be explored if GI dysfunction acts as an independent prognostic marker or simply a surrogate for uncontrolled infections. Finally, allergic inflammation was present in 20% of our cohort, consistent with the rate in the general population (27). Together, these findings establish IRF4T95R-associated disease as a CID with prominent respiratory involvement and variable but important GI disease.Of the 10 known IRF4T95R patients, only two are female (P6 and P9). Both generally exhibited a milder disease course, with neither experiencing any chronic infections, GI manifestations, or respiratory failure requiring ventilation. Ultimately, identification of additional patients will be required to determine whether biological sex modifies the clinical phenotype of IRF4 T95R.Management of IRF4T95R patients has largely relied on prevention and treatment of infection, including prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole, fluconazole, and Ig replacement therapy. Although these measures reduce infection frequency, they do not fully prevent recurrent infections or disease-related complications. Given the severity and breadth of immune dysfunction observed in these patients, HSCT should be considered on an individual basis to optimize long-term outcomes. This rationale is supported by the tissue expression pattern of IRF4, which is highly enriched in hematopoietic lineages (28). HSCT thus has the potential to restore immune function and improve survival and quality of life when appropriately tailored to patient-specific factors. The primary triggers for moving to transplant in our cohort varied, primarily centering around frequency and severity of infections. However, the observation that two patients have survived into their third and fourth decades of life without HSCT underscores that supportive care alone can confer meaningful clinical benefit in selected cases. Even with the most up-to-date treatment, patients are at lifelong risk of opportunistic infections, which can lead to significant morbidity and mortality. This highlights the need for careful, individualized risk–benefit assessment when considering HSCT.HSCT in IRF4T95R-associated disease carries a substantial risk when performed in the setting of active infection. In our cohort, transplant-related mortality occurred exclusively in patients with uncontrolled infection at the time of HSCT, reinforcing the importance of timing as the most modifiable approach to improve outcomes. Successful engraftment resulted in immune reconstitution, supporting the curative potential of HSCT when undertaken before irreversible organ damage and infectious deterioration. Conditioning approaches varied by site according to patient status and local guidelines. Generally, patients who received Treo/Flu conditioning for their first graft (P2 and P3) had worse outcomes, including endothelial damage (SOS and thrombotic microangiopathy) and death, despite reduced-toxicity regimens (29). Due to our small cohort and the complex clinical status of these patients, it is not possible to determine if an alternative conditioning approach would be more suitable. While all deaths in this cohort occurred after transplant, these were the more severe cases pre-transplant, and thus those less likely to have good outcomes owing to their already fragile health status.A notable feature of this cohort is the high rates of both graft failure and GVHD. Two patients (P2 and P4) experienced graft failure following HSCT. P2 had secondary graft failure of his first graft and primary failure of his second. Engraftment was finally achieved following the fourth HSCT. In the case of P2, active CMV and the use of third-party anti-CMV cytotoxic T lymphocytes may have been a contributing factor (30). Before transplantation, P4 was treated for anti-donor antibodies and COVID-19, which may underlie P4’s graft failure despite busulfan-based MAC. Together, graft loss in our cohort may be attributable to a wide number of factors, including underlying infection and/or inflammatory status (31, 32).All transplanted patients were affected by GVHD, possibly influenced by pre-existing active inflammation and enteropathy at the time of transplant. We previously described upregulation of CXCL13 3–4.5 times that of healthy controls in this cohort (22). Elevated CXCL13 has been linked to GVHD in both murine models and human patients (33, 34). This may thus predispose this cohort to GVHD. Furthermore, elevated CXCL13 has also been associated with inflammatory bowel disease, showing a positive correlation with inflammation severity, further supported by CXCL13 knockout mice that demonstrated reduced colitis severity (35, 36). It is plausible that elevated CXCL13 could contribute indirectly to the apparent engraftment defect in our cohort. Other biomarkers, such as ferritin and type I and II IFNs, could provide further insight. In our cohort, ferritin was normal for all patients assessed, and type II IFNs were reduced; however, type I IFNs were not assessed (22). Further work may benefit from the analysis of a range of biomarkers in this patient population, particularly before and after transplant.To date, multiple distinct IEIs affecting IRF4 have been described, each characterized by different genetic lesions, inheritance patterns, and spectra of infectious susceptibility (7) (Fig. 4 and Table S4). Accordingly, IEIs involving IRF4 should be considered as discrete clinical and molecular entities rather than grouped under the imprecise and potentially misleading label of “IRF4 deficiency.”Figure 4. full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHuman inborn errors of immunity (IEIs), which include primary immunodeficiencies, primary immune regulatory disorders, and primary atopic disorders, encompass a broad group of genetic disorders impairing immune function (1, 2, 3, 4). The phenotypes of the over 550 known IEIs span immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, autoinflammation, allergy, and malignancy (5). Tracking the clinical outcomes of these rare diseases not only informs patient diagnosis and management but also expands our understanding of fundamental human biology.Interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) are a group of nine transcription factors initially identified to play a crucial role in promoting type I interferon (IFN) production (6, 7). IRFs are transiently upregulated during antimicrobial responses, where they primarily act as transcriptional mediators in IFN-induced signaling pathways (8). Beyond IFN signaling, IRFs mediate a range of immune processes, including cytokine production and the differentiation, development, and function of lymphoid and myeloid cells (9, 10, 11, 12, 13). IRF6 is unique in that it primarily mediates epithelial function and craniofacial development rather than immune responses (7, 14, 15).IRF4, also known as MUM1, Pip, LSRIF, and ICSAT, has a vital role in immune function; however, unlike the majority of other IRFs, its primary role is not mediating IFN signaling. Instead, IRF4 is predominantly expressed in T and B cells, where it is crucial for lymphocyte development (16, 17). Multiple B cell functions rely on IRF4, including differentiation, activation, receptor editing, proliferation, class switch recombination, and plasma cell formation (9, 18, 19). Mice deficient in Irf4 exhibit impaired late-stage B cell maturation and markedly reduced serum Ig levels (9). Irf4 also plays a critical role in T cell biology, with T cell differentiation and effector fate decisions governed by graded Irf4 expression downstream of TCR signal strength (20, 21).In 2023, the IRF4 International Consortium defined a novel IEI caused by a recurrent heterozygous missense variant affecting the DNA-binding domain of IRF4 (IRF4 NM_001195286.2 c.284C>G, p.Thr95Arg, henceforth IRF4T95R) (Fig. 1 A), identified in seven patients from six unrelated kindreds (22). IRF4T95R patients presented with fully penetrant, early-onset, autosomal dominant combined immunodeficiency. Key clinical features included marked susceptibility to opportunistic infections, most notably Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). In addition, patients experienced significant viral infections, including CMV and EBV, as well as mycobacterial infections. Patients had reduced CD19+ B cells with a prominent maturation defect, with increased naïve and transitional B cells, defective plasma cell differentiation, reduced class-switched memory B cells, and agammaglobulinemia. Furthermore, T helper 17 (Th17) and T follicular helper (TFH) cells were reduced with impaired IL-12 and IFN-γ production, and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were distributed abnormally in the multidimensional space. Natural killer (NK) cells and monocytes were normal.Figure 1. Location and multimorphic mechanism of action of the IRF4 p.T95R variant. Three are found in the DNA-binding domain, including IRF4 p.T95R, and two are located in the IRF association domain. (B) IRF4 p.T95R demonstrates unusual multimorphic effects: hypermorphic through increased DNA-binding affinity, hypomorphic with poor expression of canonical IRF4 target genes, and neomorphic with expression of non-canonical targets such as CXCL13. Panel B illustrates the multimorphic effects of the IRF4 p.T95R variant, including loss of function, gain of function, and new function, with specific impacts on gene binding and expression.Biochemically, IRF4T95R protein levels were normal in multiple cell types, but B cells transduced with IRF4T95R demonstrated abnormal IRF4 localization, impaired class switch recombination, and reduced plasma cell differentiation. DNA-binding affinity was increased, likely due to the change to positively charged arginine, allowing more and longer interactions with DNA, resulting in an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. papers.title_original: IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency: Clinical features and transplant outcomes

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to characterize the clinical features and transplant outcomes of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, a rare disorder associated with severe susceptibility to infections. The background highlights the need to understand the disease course and treatment outcomes in affected individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 10 patients with the IRF4 p.T95R variant, including four who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Patients spanned four continents, with disease onset uniformly early (<1 year) and a male predominance (8/10).
analysis.methods: Patients received HSCT with varying donor sources, conditioning regimens, and immunosuppression protocols. One patient had multiple HSCT donors, with the initial graft from a matched unrelated donor and subsequent grafts from the same mismatched related donor. Outcomes were evaluated based on survival and complications following transplant.
analysis.main_results: Two patients survived with a median follow-up of 37 months, while two died at 9 and 12.5 months post-HSCT. One death was due to multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection, and another was from thrombotic microangiopathy-associated multi-organ failure. Both patients had active infections (CMV and Cryptosporidium) at the time of transplant.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency is characterized by marked susceptibility to a broad spectrum of infections, with HSCT outcomes being mixed. This study provides the most comprehensive description of the disorder to date.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the management of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, particularly regarding the risks and outcomes of HSCT in the context of active infections. They also highlight the importance of early diagnosis and tailored immunosuppression strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective nature and the small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the lack of prospective data and the potential for unmeasured confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the clinical features and transplant outcomes of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, a rare genetic disorder causing severe susceptibility to infections. Four of the 10 patients underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), with mixed results: two survived, while two died from complications related to active infections at the time of transplant. The authors interpret that this condition is marked by broad immune dysfunction, with HSCT outcomes influenced by the presence of concurrent infections. The findings contribute to understanding the disease course and treatment challenges, emphasizing the need for careful management of infections in affected individuals. However, the study's retrospective design and small sample size limit the strength of the evidence, suggesting a moderate confidence level in the conclusions.

elements_zh.methods: 患者接受不同供体来源、预处理方案和免疫抑制方案的 HSCT。一名患者有多个 HSCT 供体,最初的移植物来自匹配的无关供体,随后的移植物来自同一不匹配的相关供体。根据移植后的存活率和并发症评估结果。
elements_zh.main_results: 两名患者在中位随访 37 个月后存活,两名患者在 HSCT 后 9 个月和 12.5 个月死亡。一名死亡是由于多重耐药肺炎克雷伯菌感染,另一名死亡是由于血栓性微血管病相关的多器官衰竭。两名患者在移植时均存在活动性感染(CMV 和隐孢子虫)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,IRF4 p.T95R 联合免疫缺陷的特点是对广谱感染具有明显的易感性,而 HSCT 的结果则参差不齐。这项研究提供了迄今为止对该疾病最全面的描述。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 IRF4 p.T95R 联合免疫缺陷患者的管理提供了信息,特别是关于活动性感染情况下 HSCT 的风险和结果。他们还强调了早期 诊断 和定制免疫抑制策略的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性和样本量小而受到限制,这可能会影响结果的普遍性。由于缺乏前瞻性数据并且可能存在未测量的混杂因素,证据是中等的。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to characterize the clinical features and transplant outcomes of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, a rare disorder associated with severe susceptibility to infections. The background highlights the need to understand the disease course and treatment outcomes in affected individuals.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 10 patients with the IRF4 p.T95R variant, including four who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Patients spanned four continents, with disease onset uniformly early (<1 year) and a male predominance (8/10).
analysis_en.methods: Patients received HSCT with varying donor sources, conditioning regimens, and immunosuppression protocols. One patient had multiple HSCT donors, with the initial graft from a matched unrelated donor and subsequent grafts from the same mismatched related donor. Outcomes were evaluated based on survival and complications following transplant.
analysis_en.main_results: Two patients survived with a median follow-up of 37 months, while two died at 9 and 12.5 months post-HSCT. One death was due to multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infection, and another was from thrombotic microangiopathy-associated multi-organ failure. Both patients had active infections (CMV and Cryptosporidium) at the time of transplant.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency is characterized by marked susceptibility to a broad spectrum of infections, with HSCT outcomes being mixed. This study provides the most comprehensive description of the disorder to date.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the management of patients with IRF4 p.T95R combined immunodeficiency, particularly regarding the risks and outcomes of HSCT in the context of active infections. They also highlight the importance of early diagnosis and tailored immunosuppression strategies.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective nature and the small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the lack of prospective data and the potential for unmeasured confounding factors.
